name: Telugu
where: Andhra Pradesh and Telangana — Hyderabad, Vijayawada, Visakhapatnam — plus a huge US diaspora, especially in tech.
script_note: Round, looping letters — the curves come from writing on palm leaves, where straight cuts would tear the leaf. Left to right and fully phonetic: 16 vowels (short and long e/o matter!) and all the consonant rows Hindi has, plus extras like ళ and a second R (ఱ).
difficulty: US Foreign Service Institute Category III (about 1,100 hours to professional proficiency) — grouped with Hindi. The script is phonetic and verbs are regular; the new habits are agglutination (long words glued from small parts) and inclusive/exclusive 'we'.

sov.en: I eat rice (word-for-word: I · rice · eat)

gender_title: Gender lives in the verb (third person)
gender_note: Telugu nouns don't force masculine/feminine on you, but third-person verbs agree: వాడు తింటాడు (he eats), ఆమె తింటుంది (she eats). First and second person never split — నేను తింటాను is said by men and women alike.
present_note: One verb, seven endings: the ending tells you WHO — and in the third person, their gender. Formal మీరు shares its ending with they.
negation_note: Telugu negates by swapping the verb ending: నేను తింటాను (I eat) → నేను తినను (tinanu, I don't eat). No extra word — the ending does the work.
counting_note: Telugu counts directly — but people get special number-words:
survival_trio: X ఎక్కడ ఉంది? (where is X?), ఛార్జీ ఎంత? (how much?), ఇక్కడ ఆపండి (stop here). These three handle 80% of travel.
bargaining_script: ఇది ఎంత? → చాలా ఖరీదు! → కొంచెం తగ్గించండి → సరే, తీసుకుంటాను. Smile through all four steps.

vowels.hint: a as in 'about' — a short neutral uh
ru as in 'rude' — rare, Sanskrit loanwords only
long ṛ — almost never seen outside dictionaries
SHORT e, as in 'pen' — contrasts with ఏ below
LONG ay, as in 'say' — length changes meaning!
SHORT o, as in 'pot' — contrasts with ఓ below
LONG o, as in 'go' — length changes meaning!
breathy h at word end — rare

consonants.hint: k with a puff of air
g with a puff of air
ch as in 'church' (coastal districts say 'tsa' — same letter, local music)
ch with a puff of air
j with a puff of air
retroflex t with a puff of air
retroflex d with a puff of air
dental t with a puff of air (never 'th' as in 'thin')
dental d with a puff of air
p with a puff of air (often 'f' in city speech)
b with a puff of air
trilled r — rolled, unlike the tapped Hindi/Marathi r
same sound as శ in daily speech
retroflex L, like Marathi ळ — tongue curled back
a SECOND, tapped R (బండి ర, bandi-ra) — rare in print, alive in speech

greetings.note: Literally 'I'll come (back)' — the stayer answers మళ్ళీ రండి (come again)

pronouns.note: మనం (manaṁ) = we-INCLUDING-you — Telugu splits what Hindi/English merge
వాడు (vāḍu) is the familiar 'he' — friends only

verbs.note: Formal books write వెళ్ళుతాను — streets say వెళ్తాను
Irregular: the root changes (రా → వస్తా) — just memorize it
More common: నాకు X ఇష్టం (I like X) — see daily phrases
పడుకోవడం (paḍukōvaḍaṁ) = lie down / go to bed

time_words.note: Street Telugu — formal books say సమయం ఎంత?

family.note: Telugu splits siblings by age — అన్న (elder) vs తమ్ముడు (younger)

food_words.note: The fun long word — shops just say ఆలూ

colors.note: Colours never change for gender or number — say them as listed

core_nouns.note: Street word — పాఠశాల (pāṭhaśāla) is the formal one

daily_phrases.note: కావాలి (want/need) always works this way: నాకు X కావాలి

culture.en: The Telugu harvest festival (January) — kites on every terrace, sugarcane in every hand, pongal pots boiling over in the courtyard.
Telugu New Year — the sweet-bitter ugadi pachadi teaches the year's first lesson: life is a mix, taste it all.
Telangana's flower festival — nine nights of stacked marigolds and circle songs. Women build it, everyone sings it.
Ashada folk festival for Mahankali — pots of offering carried dancing through old Hyderabad's lanes.
The dum-cooked legend — Paradise vs Bawarchi is a friendly war. Pick a side, then eat at both.

classifiers.note: one book — number + noun, no extras
two fruits — counting form as listed
three people — ముగ్గురు is the people-form of three; Telugu numbers change for humans

lines.t: నమస్కారం! నేను అర్జున్. మీరు ఎలా ఉన్నారు?
lines.r: Namaskāraṁ! Nēnu Arjun. Mīru elā unnāru?
lines.hi: नमस्ते! मैं अर्जुन हूँ। आप कैसे हैं?
lines.en: Hello! I'm Arjun. How are you?

lines.hi: मैं ठीक हूँ, धन्यवाद। आप कहाँ से हैं?
lines.en: I'm fine, thank you. Where are you from?

lines.t: నేను చెన్నై నుండి. నేను తెలుగు నేర్చుకుంటున్నాను.
lines.r: Nēnu Chennai nunḍi. Nēnu telugu nērchukunṭunnānu.
lines.hi: मैं चेन्नई से हूँ। मैं तेलुगु सीख रहा हूँ।
lines.en: I'm from Chennai. I'm learning Telugu.
Brother, one tea please. (అన్నా = elder brother — everyone calls the vendor అన్నా)
Excuse me, where is the station?

lines.hi: नहीं, पास ही है। पाँच मिनट।

quiz.explain: నమస్కారం (namaskāraṁ) is the standard formal hello — to elders, officials, anyone you respect.

quiz.q: How do you say 'thank you' in Telugu?
quiz.explain: ధన్యవాదాలు (dhanyavādālu). క్షమించండి is excuse-me/sorry — don't mix them.

quiz.q: Telugu ఎ and ఏ differ in…
quiz.a: vowel length (short e vs long ē)
opts: vowel length (short e vs long ē)
quiz.explain: Telugu doubles its e and o: short vs long changes meaning. Same for ఒ/ఓ. Train your ear from day one.
మీరు (mīru) is formal 'you' — safe with every stranger.
ఐదు (aidu) = 5.
పది (padi) = 10. ఇరవై is 20, వంద is 100.
ఇరవై (iravai) = 20 — its own word, like English 'twenty'.
వంద (vanda) = 100 in counting; నూరు (nūru) appears in compounds.
అన్నం (annaṁ) is cooked rice — the centre of the Telugu plate. Uncooked rice is బియ్యం.
చేప (chēpa) = fish. Coastal Andhra runs on fish and rice.
ఒక = one, ఇవ్వండి = give (polite). The full polite ordering pattern.
ఎక్కడ (ekkaḍa) = where. X ఎక్కడ ఉంది? is the whole direction toolkit in three words.
కుడి (kuḍi) = to the right. Left is ఎడమ, straight is సరాసరి.
ఛార్జీ (chārjī) = fare, ఎంత = how much. Ask the auto driver before you sit down.

quiz.q: నేను అన్నం తింటాను. The word order is…
quiz.explain: Telugu is subject–object–verb: నేను అన్నం తింటాను. The verb always goes last.
మీరు (mīru) is formal and safe everywhere. నువ్వు to a stranger is rude.
తినను (tinanu) is the negative ending: తింటాను → తినను. No extra word — the ending does the work.
తింటుంది (tinṭundi) — Telugu verbs agree in the third person. 'He eats' is తింటాడు.
నా (nā) = my, పేరు = name. నా పేరు లక్ష్మి = my name is Lakshmi.
నేర్చుకుంటున్నాను is present continuous: right now, in progress. Say it to any Telugu person and watch them smile.
పుస్తకం (pustakaṁ) = book. ఒక పుస్తకం = one book.
ఇల్లు (illu) = house/home. ఇంట్లో = at home (లో = in/at).
ఇది (this) + ఎంత (how much). The market survival sentence.
రేపు (rēpu) = tomorrow. Yesterday is నిన్న — Telugu splits them cleanly.

lines.hi: डॉक्टर, दो दिन से बुख़ार है।

lines.en: Thank you, doctor. Any diet restrictions?

advanced_modules.lede: Body, symptoms and the clinic — Telugu for staying well.

quiz.explain: జ్వరం (jvaraṁ) = fever — నాకు జ్వరం (I have a fever).
డాక్టర్ (ḍākṭar) = doctor.
ఒంట్లో బాగాలేదు — ఒళ్ళు = body.
మందుల దుకాణం ఎక్కడ? — ఎక్కడ = where.
quiz.q: Ask where the pharmacy is. You say…

quiz.explain: గుండె (guṇḍe) = heart.
పథ్యం (pathyaṁ) — the doctor's diet rules.
త్వరగా కోలుకోండి — త్వరగా = soon.
నోరు తెరవండి = open your mouth — నోరు = mouth.
quiz.q: The doctor says 'open your mouth'. She says…

quiz.explain: ఇంజెక్షన్ (iñjekshan) — injection; సూది = needle.
విశ్రాంతి తీసుకోండి — విశ్రాంతి = rest.

కంప్యూటర్ (kampyūṭar) = computer.
సమయానికి రండి — సమయం = time.

ఈమెయిల్ పంపండి — పంపండి = send.

మంచి పని! — మంచి = good.
